title: A real body raised
hookLine: the churches hold the resurrection was bodily, not only a feeling

lines: THEY THINK THEY SEE A SPIRIT.
HE TOOK IT, AND DID EAT.
cards: A piece of broiled fish, and some honeycomb. That's what's on the table in a room in Jerusalem, on the evening of the first Easter, in Luke's telling. The disciples are terrified.

Jesus is standing among them, and they're sure they're seeing a spirit. So he asks a homely question: have you got anything here to eat? They hand him the fish, and Luke says, "he took it, and did eat before them."
Ghosts don't eat supper. Day five hundred ninety sat at this same table. Today, the question underneath it.

teach.b: These last days asked what the cross does. Today: what is Easter? Some people today describe the resurrection as a feeling: grief turning to hope, Jesus living on in memory.
The Gospels insist on something harder.
In Luke, Jesus says: "Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have."
In John's Gospel, Thomas won't believe until he puts his finger in the wounds. After eight days, Jesus is there again: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands."
The scars are still there. Raised, and recognizably the same body. And yet not simply a corpse come back.
In John, he stands among them when the doors are shut. Two friends walk beside him on a road and don't recognize him at first.
Paul tries to name it in his first letter to Corinth: "It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body."

teach.h: A SPIRITUAL BODY: REAL AND NEW.
teach.b: Christian teachers have read a spiritual body not as a body made of mist, but as one wholly alive with God's Spirit: real, and new.
And Paul won't treat this as a side detail: "if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain."
The old creeds confess that the dead will rise too; the Apostles' Creed calls it "the Resurrection of the body." Christians differ on how to picture a raised body. These texts all speak of a body.

how: Christians who say the Apostles' Creed in worship confess the resurrection of the body, the Nicene Creed looks for the resurrection of the dead, and Easter Sunday celebrates Christ's bodily rising from the tomb.

games.q: what does “a real body raised” mean?
o: Jesus appearing as a spirit who could not be touched
a ghostly vision seen only in the disciples' dreams
Jesus raised in a real body, scarred, yet made new

games.q: a body, not a ghost — tap the pairs.
p: he took it, and did eat before them

s: in Luke, the disciples first think they're seeing a spirit
they were terrified. Jesus says a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have.
a spiritual body, in Paul, means a body made of mist
Christian teachers read it as a body wholly alive with God's Spirit: real, and new.
the raised Jesus has no wounds
he tells Thomas to reach his finger and behold his hands. the scars are still there.

games.q: you're Thomas. you said you'd only believe if you touched the wounds. now Jesus stands in front of you and says, reach hither thy finger. what does John say you do?
o: reach out and touch the wounds.
say, my Lord and my God.
games.why: John reports Thomas saying, "my Lord and my God." the Gospel never says he actually touched.

practice: Rest one hand in the other and feel the weight, the warmth, the lines in the palm, any scar you've collected. In the Easter story, the hands that were wounded are the ones raised; nothing is thrown away.
If you pray, thank God for this body as it is; if you don't, just let it be here, and be noticed.

wordCard.voice: A real body raised. The churches' confession that Easter is about a body: touchable, scarred, eating fish, and made new.

carryVoice: Your line: a body, not a ghost. Scars and all. See you tomorrow.
